title: Best No-Code AI App Builders for Open-Source Models in 2026 (Kimi K3, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM)
summary: Which no-code AI app builders run open-source models like Kimi K3, DeepSeek, Qwen and GLM in 2026? 8 tools compared, with GPU sizing, licenses and host speeds.
body_markdown:
> **TL;DR:** Open weights are not open-source code, and not "runs on my laptop" either: Kimi K3 is a 1.56 TB checkpoint, too big for an 8x H100 or 8x B200 GPU node. Use a builder that runs the model or takes your host key. Taskade Genesis runs DeepSeek V4 Pro on every paid plan, no key needed.[Try it free →](https://www.taskade.com/create?entry_kind=content&source=blog&entry=%2Fblog%2Fopen-model-builders)


**The best AI app builder for open-source models in 2026 depends on who runs the model.**[Taskade Genesis](https://www.taskade.com/ai/apps) runs DeepSeek V4 Pro, MiniMax M3 and Nemotron 3 Super on every paid plan with no API key, and Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3 on Max and Enterprise.[Dify](https://dify.ai/) ,[n8n](https://n8n.io/) and[Langflow](https://www.langflow.org/) connect the same models through your own host key or your own server.


Open-weight models closed much of the gap in 2026. Taskade's model docs rate[Kimi K3](https://www.taskade.com/models/kimi-k3) and GLM 5.3 at frontier intelligence, DeepSeek V4 Pro runs on every paid plan, and their weights are a download away on[Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3) . That raises a practical question for anyone who builds apps without code: **which builders let you pick an open-weight model, and how?**


This guide answers it for eight tools, ranked by how directly a non-developer can put an open model to work. One note before the list, because search engines mix the two up: **open weights are not open-source code.** A builder whose code is open source can still call a closed model, and a closed builder can run an open-weight model. This post is about the second case: open-weight *models* inside hosted builders.


Every plan and model claim below was checked on the vendor's own docs or pricing page on October 20, 2026. Every model size, license and parameter count was read from the model's own Hugging Face repository on the same day, so you can check our arithmetic.


Here is what this guide covers, in the order most readers need it:


- **The ranked list** : eight builders, what each one is best at, and the open models to start with in each.
- **A builder-by-model matrix** : which tools run Kimi K3, DeepSeek, Qwen and GLM.
- **A self-hosting sizing table** : checkpoint size and the smallest GPU setup for twelve open-weight releases.
- **A license table** : which open models carry revenue or display clauses.

- **A step-by-step walkthrough** : building an app on an open-weight model in Taskade.

## What does "open-weight" mean, and why run one inside a builder?


**An open-weight model is a trained AI model whose weights anyone can download.** You get the file, not a password to someone's API. That gives you three things a closed model cannot: price competition between many hosts, a choice of model per job, and no lock-in, because the same weights run on any provider that serves them.


The license still decides what you may do with the file, and it varies. DeepSeek V4 ships under MIT for code and weights. Qwen's smaller open models use Apache 2.0, and the 2.4T Qwen3.8 flagship uses a custom license. Kimi K3 uses Moonshot's own **Kimi K3 License** , which is not MIT (the earlier K2 line used a modified MIT). Our[open-source LLM guide](https://www.taskade.com/blog/open-source-llms) covers each license in detail.


### Open weights vs open source: what you actually download


**Most models people call "open source" in 2026 are open-weight models.** You get the trained weights and usually the code to run them, but not the training data or the full training recipe. The Open Source Initiative's[Open Source AI Definition](https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition) , published in October 2024, asks for all of those pieces. Few frontier releases meet that bar, which is why this guide says "open-weight" when it means a model file you can download.


Release type Weights Training code and data License Examples (October 2026)


Closed model No, API only No Terms of service GPT-6.1 Sol, Qwen 3.7 Plus and Max


Open weights, standard license Yes No MIT or Apache 2.0 DeepSeek V4, GLM 5.2, Qwen3.6, Qwen3.8-27B, gpt-oss


Open weights, custom license Yes No Lab's own terms Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 2.4T, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3, Nemotron 3 Super


Fully open source AI Yes Yes, or detailed data information OSI-approved Rare at frontier scale


For someone building an app, the license column matters more than the label. It decides whether a host may sell the model to you, and whether a large product must credit the lab. The[open-source models wiki entry](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/open-source-models) and our[history of open-source LLMs](https://www.taskade.com/blog/open-source-llm-history) trace how the terms drifted apart. This short explainer covers the same split from a developer's angle:


**Open weights do not mean you can run the model.** Kimi K3 has 2.8 trillion parameters (2.78T exact). Its checkpoint on Hugging Face is about 1.56 TB, in native MXFP4 weights with MXFP8 activations. Every byte of that must sit in GPU memory before the first token comes out. Here is the arithmetic:


```text
CAN I RUN KIMI K3 MYSELF?            checkpoint ~1.56 TB, plus room for cache
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Hardware                  GPU memory          Fits the weights?
Laptop or one RTX card    8 to 32 GB          no   (about 50x too small)
8x H100  (80 GB each)     640 GB              no   (less than half)
8x B200  (180 GB each)    1.44 TB             no   (short before any cache)
8x B300  (288 GB each)    about 2.3 TB        YES  (one node, ~0.7 TB left
for cache and batches)
Host API or a builder     someone else's      YES  (pay per token or plan)
Smaller open models are different: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B uses 3B parameters per
token and runs on a single consumer GPU.


```


So for most teams, the realistic paths are a hosted builder that buys tokens for you, or a builder that takes a key from a model host such as[Together AI](https://www.together.ai/) ,[Fireworks](https://fireworks.ai/) ,[OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/) or[Baseten](https://www.baseten.co/) . ## Should you build on an open-weight or a closed model?


**Choose an open-weight model when price, choice of host or control over data matters more than the last few points of quality on one task.** Choose a closed model when a single job needs the strongest model of the month and you do not want to compare hosts. Most apps mix both. A builder that lets you pick a model per agent turns the either-or into a setting.


The flowchart walks the four questions that decide it for most teams:



In Taskade the choice is per surface, not per workspace. One[AI agent](https://www.taskade.com/agents) can run DeepSeek V4 Pro, another can run Kimi K3, and the builder chat can stay on Auto. Our guide to[model routing](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/platform/model-routing) explains how Auto picks a model for each request.

## The 8 Best No-Code Builders for Open-Weight Models


### 1.[Taskade Genesis](https://www.taskade.com/ai/apps) : Best for apps with agents and automations on open models, no keys needed


Taskade Genesis builds a working app from a prompt, with agents, automations and a database. Its[model catalog](https://www.taskade.com/docs/models/custom-engine) offers frontier models from top AI labs. **Auto** is the default, and you can pin a model in the builder chat or on an agent.


On Taskade credits, no key:


- **DeepSeek V4 Pro** , **MiniMax M3** and **Nemotron 3 Super** : every paid plan.
- **Kimi K3** , **Kimi K2.7 Code** and **Kimi K2.6** : Max and Enterprise. The[Kimi docs](https://www.taskade.com/docs/models/kimi) rate K3 Slow, Frontier intelligence, Medium cost.
- **GLM 5.3** and **GLM 5.2** : Max and Enterprise.


The Qwen 3.7 models in the picker are Alibaba's API-only tier, not open weights.


With your own key ([BYOK](https://www.taskade.com/learn/account/enterprise-byok) ), a **Together AI key** on Business and up serves Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, MiniMax M3 and Qwen 3.7 Plus to custom agents and Ask Agent, and a **Groq key** on the same plans serves gpt-oss. Your plan includes agent steps on your key each month, and each agent step after that uses one fixed step fee in Taskade credits. In automations, Groq and OpenRouter provider steps need Business and up, and each step uses one fixed step fee in Taskade credits. The[key providers page](https://www.taskade.com/models/providers) lists what each key serves.


**Open models to start with:**[DeepSeek V4 Pro](https://www.taskade.com/models/deepseek-v4-pro) for everyday builds and edits on Pro, because it runs on every paid plan with no key. Move one agent to[Kimi K3](https://www.taskade.com/models/kimi-k3) on Max or Enterprise when the job needs long-context reasoning and you can wait for a slower, more thorough build.


**Strengths:** open models on every paid plan with no key, beside your agents and automations. **Trade-offs:** Kimi K3 on credits needs Max ($100/mo billed annually), and Taskade EVE builds and edits run on your key only when you pick a model under **Your keys** , with one fixed step fee in credits for each step. Free starts with no AI credits. Pro is $10/mo billed annually ([pricing](https://www.taskade.com/pricing) ).


### 2.[Dify](https://dify.ai/) : Best for LLM apps, RAG and chatflows on any model provider


Dify is an open platform for LLM apps: chatbots, retrieval over your documents, and visual workflows. Model access comes through provider plugins. The official plugin repo on GitHub includes plugins for **DeepSeek** , **Moonshot** , **Zhipu AI** (GLM), **Tongyi** (Qwen), **Ollama** , **Together AI** , **Fireworks** , **Groq** , **OpenRouter** , **SiliconFlow** and a generic **OpenAI-API-compatible** plugin, plus **Xinference** and **LocalAI** for your own servers. Its compatible-plugin README lists deepseek-v4-pro, deepseek-v4-flash and kimi-k2.7-code as examples.


Dify Cloud has a free Sandbox plan with 200 message credits, a Professional plan at $590 per workspace per year, and a Team plan at $1,590 per workspace per year. Dify's pricing page says you can switch to your own API key when message credits run out. The self-hosted Community Edition is free.


**Open models to start with:** the DeepSeek plugin for a first chat or retrieval app, since the MIT-licensed V4 models are served by many hosts. Add the Tongyi plugin for Qwen, or the Together AI or Fireworks plugin to reach Kimi K3 and GLM through one host account.


**Strengths:** the widest provider list of any tool here, and real retrieval and workflow features for production chatbots. Self-hosting keeps every prompt on your own servers. **Trade-offs:** you bring the model key for open models, and the license is a modified Apache 2.0 that forbids running Dify as a multi-tenant service without a commercial license. Plan for that before you resell a Dify-based product. Dify focuses on LLM apps and chat interfaces, so a larger business app with its own screens needs another tool beside it.


### 3.[n8n](https://n8n.io/) : Best for workflow automation with dedicated open-model nodes


n8n is a workflow automation tool with an AI Agent node and a set of chat model sub-nodes. The n8n docs list dedicated nodes for **DeepSeek** , **Moonshot Kimi** , **Groq** , **OpenRouter** , **Mistral Cloud** , **Ollama** , **Qwen Cloud** , **MiniMax** and **NVIDIA Nemotron** , among others. The DeepSeek node loads models from your account, so "you'll only see the models available to your account." The Ollama Chat Model node connects to a local or remote Ollama server.


n8n Cloud starts at €20/mo billed annually for 2,500 workflow executions on Starter, and €50/mo billed annually for 10,000 on Pro. The self-hosted Community Edition runs under n8n's Sustainable Use License, a fair-code license rather than an OSI open-source one. The pricing page notes that the self-hosted AI Assistant uses your own API key.


**Open models to start with:** the DeepSeek Chat Model node for low-cost text steps, and the Moonshot Kimi Chat Model node when an agent step needs a long context. For a model without its own node, the OpenRouter node reaches many open-weight models through one key.


**Strengths:** n8n plans count workflow executions, not individual steps, and its node library covers a wide range of business apps. Open-model nodes drop into any workflow, so one step can call DeepSeek and the next can write to your CRM. **Trade-offs:** you need a key from each model host, and n8n builds workflows, not apps with screens. The plain Ollama Model node lacks tool support, so use the Ollama Chat Model node with the AI Agent node.


### 4.[MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/) : Best for a hosted model catalog with no API keys


MindStudio is a no-code builder for AI agents and workflows with a very large hosted model catalog. On October 20, 2026 its models page listed **Kimi K3** and **Kimi K2.6** , eleven **DeepSeek** models, thirty-eight **Qwen** models, **Llama 4 Scout** , and **GPT OSS 120B** and **20B** served via Groq. The page says the models are available with "no API keys required."


Pricing is a plan plus usage. Free is $0 plus usage, with one agent and 1,000 runs per month. Individual is $20/mo, or $16/mo billed yearly, plus usage, with unlimited agents and runs. MindStudio's FAQ states that it does not mark up model costs: "You pay EXACTLY the same price as getting your own API keys directly from model providers." You can still bring your own keys if you prefer.


**Open models to start with:** run one prompt across Kimi K3, a DeepSeek model and a Qwen model, then keep the cheapest one that passes. Because model usage is passed through at the provider's rate, the test costs what the hosts charge. GPT OSS 120B on Groq is the speed option.


**Strengths:** the broadest open-model menu with zero key setup, and transparent pass-through model pricing. It is a good place to compare several open models on one prompt. **Trade-offs:** usage is billed on top of the plan, so a busy agent's bill tracks its token count. MindStudio builds agents and workflows rather than full apps with a shared database, and the catalog marks older models such as Kimi K2.7 Code as deprecated, so check status before you pin one.


### 5.[Langflow](https://www.langflow.org/) : Best free visual agent builder you host yourself


Langflow is a visual builder for agents and retrieval flows, released under the MIT license. In Langflow 1.12, a core **Language Model** component supports many providers through a global **Models** setting. For anything not built in, you set the **OpenAI Compatible** provider to point at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which covers Together AI, Fireworks, OpenRouter and most other open-model hosts. Langflow also ships an **Ollama** bundle for local models and a **DeepSeek** bundle whose output can drive an Agent component.


Langflow is free to download and self-host. You pay for the server and for the model host behind each key. The project is very active on GitHub, with commits landing the day we checked.


**Open models to start with:** the DeepSeek bundle for a first agent flow, then the OpenAI Compatible provider pointed at Together AI or Fireworks for Kimi K3 or GLM. For a laptop test, the Ollama bundle runs gpt-oss-20b or a 4-bit Qwen3.6 build locally.


**Strengths:** an MIT license with no multi-tenant clause, and a clean drag-and-drop canvas that developers can extend in Python. The OpenAI-compatible route means a new open model works the day a host lists it. **Trade-offs:** one API key per provider, and that key must reach every model you plan to use. Langflow is a developer-leaning tool: you host it, secure it and connect it to a front end yourself.


### 6.[Kimi Build](https://www.kimi.com/) : Best for trying Kimi K3 in the lab's own builder


Kimi Build is Moonshot's own app and website builder inside Kimi Agent, and Kimi's help center says it runs on Kimi K3. You describe a site in plain language, or upload a design mockup or a screen recording, and it builds a full-stack site with a backend, a database and sign-in. A visual database panel lets you view, edit and delete records.


Sites stay preview-only until you publish. Published sites get a subdomain on` ok.kimi.link` , and you can download a complete project package, front end and back end, to host yourself. The help center notes that Kimi account login and the cloud database do not move with exported code, so a self-hosted copy needs its own login system and database. The help article does not state which plan or quota you need, so read Kimi's membership page first.


**Open models to start with:** Kimi K3 is the only option, so the question is fit, not choice. Use Kimi Build to see what a 2.8-trillion-parameter open model makes from a mockup, then export the code if you want the site on your own host.


**Strengths:** the most direct way to see what Kimi K3 builds, from the lab that trained it, and multimodal input from a mockup or a screen recording. Code export gives you an exit. **Trade-offs:** one model family only, so you cannot switch to DeepSeek or GLM for a cheaper step. Kimi Build makes websites rather than a workspace of agents and automations, and plan details sit on a separate membership page.


### 7.[Dyad](https://www.dyad.sh/) : Best for local, private app building on your own machine


Dyad is a free desktop app that builds web apps from plain-language prompts. Project files stay on your disk, and the app runs with no account. Dyad supports your own keys for "OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, LM Studio, and more," and it works offline with local models through[Ollama](https://ollama.com/) or[LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai/) . Outside its` src/pro/` folder, Dyad's code is licensed under Apache 2.0.


Free is $0 with your own key. Pro is $20/mo and adds Pro modes for large codebases and 200 credits per month. Max is $79/mo with 900 credits.


**Open models to start with:** gpt-oss-20b, whose 14 GB checkpoint fits a 16 GB GPU, or a 4-bit Qwen3.6-35B-A3B build on a 24 GB card through Ollama. For the large open models, add a key from a supported host and let the host run them.


**Strengths:** the simplest way on this list to build with a local open model and no internet at all, which suits private data and travel. A mid-size open model like Qwen3.6-35B-A3B fits a single consumer GPU. **Trade-offs:** local models are far smaller than Kimi K3 or DeepSeek V4 Pro, so expect simpler apps. You manage hosting and deployment for what Dyad builds. Your laptop does the model work, so speed and model size depend on your own hardware.


### 8.[Bolt](https://bolt.new/) : Best for watching open models in a code-first builder


Bolt is a browser-based builder that writes full app code. On September 14, 2026 it launched **Bolt Forge** , an agent that runs only on open-source models: GLM 5.3 Flash (Bolt's recommended starting point), GLM 5.3, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro. Bolt's support page says Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro use up Forge usage faster than the GLM models.


The preview ran from September 14 to October 14, 2026, with up to 50x more usage for individual Pro plans. Bolt's support page says Pro subscribers lose Forge access after October 14, and Lite subscribers ($9/mo, waitlist) who joined by then keep it. Forge is not available on Teams or Enterprise. Builders opt in to share de-identified sessions, which go into datasets licensed to AI developers, with Arcee AI as the first licensee ([Bolt's Forge post](https://bolt.new/blog/what-is-bolt-forge) ). Bolt itself has a free plan, and Pro starts at $18/mo billed annually.


**Open models to start with:** GLM 5.3 Flash, Bolt's recommended starting point, which uses Forge usage slower than Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro. If your Forge access has ended, Bolt's Standard and Max agents remain available for the same projects.


**Strengths:** Forge puts four open models in one agent picker next to Bolt's Standard and Max agents, so you can compare and switch back in one click. Bolt is open about the trade: its support page states which models use usage faster. **Trade-offs:** on October 20, 2026, Forge access depends on how you subscribed, and its usage is tied to training-data consent. Check Bolt's support page for the current lineup before you plan around it.


> **Not ranked: Flowise.** Flowise stopped feature development on July 29, 2026, and[announced its wind-down](https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise/discussions/6727) on August 13, 2026. The team archived its GitHub repository, and the core team's support ended on August 31, 2026. The code stays Apache 2.0, and the team encourages forks, but we do not recommend new projects on it.

## TSK-1: how each open-weight family builds real apps


**In TSK-1, Taskade's hands-on app-building test, the DeepSeek family leads on design, Kimi K3 posted the most reliable round, GLM showed the best judgment on an unclear brief, and MiniMax M3 was not scored.** Every result below comes from a dated round on the[TSK-1 hub](https://www.taskade.com/tsk) . ### Why total parameters, not active ones, set the memory bill


**A mixture-of-experts model computes with a small slice of its weights per token but must keep every expert in GPU memory.** Kimi K3 uses about 104 billion of its 2.78 trillion parameters for each token. At production batch sizes, though, different requests route to different experts, so every expert is busy at some instant. Swapping experts in and out of memory would break any latency promise. So total parameters set how many[GPUs](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/infrastructure/gpu) you need, and active parameters set how much math each token costs. Our[mixture-of-experts entry](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/mixture-of-experts) shows the routing step by step.


Baseten's engineers walk through the same constraint for Kimi K3, along with how they split the model across eight GPUs with tensor and expert parallelism:


The two parallelism styles trade latency for throughput. **Tensor parallelism** (TP8) shards every layer across all eight GPUs, which gives the best single-user latency and the most traffic between GPUs. **Tensor plus expert parallelism** keeps attention sharded and places whole experts on specific GPUs, which raises throughput. Hosts also add or remove copies of busy experts at run time to balance load. None of this is visible to you in a builder, but it is why two hosts serve the same weights at very different speeds.

## Why open-weight models are cheaper to serve


**Open-weight models are often cheaper per token because of how they are built and how they are sold.** Three design choices cut the compute per token, and open distribution lets many hosts compete on one set of weights. Kimi K3 shows all four effects at once. Our guide to[AI inference](https://www.taskade.com/blog/ai-inference-explained) explains each step in depth.


**1. Mixture of experts: total parameters set memory, active parameters set compute.** Kimi K3 has 896 routed experts. Each token goes to 16 routed experts plus 2 shared ones, about 104B parameters, or about 3.7% of the 2.78T total. So each token costs roughly what a 104B dense model costs to compute. The catch: at production batch sizes, every expert is busy at some instant, so all 2.78T must stay in GPU memory. That is why, in the sizing block near the top of this guide, only the 8x B300 node fits the weights.


**2. Hybrid attention keeps the cache small.** Kimi K3 has 93 layers. 69 use Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), a linear attention that keeps a fixed-size state per sequence (about 217 MB in BF16 across the model). 24 use Gated MLA, which keeps a per-token cache of about 13.5 KiB in FP8. A full 1,048,576-token window therefore needs about 13.5 GiB of per-token cache, far less than a model where every layer caches every token. The trade-off: a cached prompt prefix resumes exactly for MLA, but the KDA layers resume only from the nearest saved state, so prefix caching is coarser.


**3. Speculative decoding raises per-user speed.** A small draft model proposes several tokens, and the large model checks them in one pass. Baseten names EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark as speculator options for K3. A speculator trains on the target model's own hidden states, so it arrives after the model is live.


**4. Same weights, many hosts.** Because anyone can serve the weights, hosts compete.[Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/kimi-k3/providers) measured Kimi K3 output speed on October 20, 2026:


That is about a 10x spread for identical weights. Speed is a property of the host, not of the model, which is why a builder that can switch hosts or take your key gives you a lever a closed model does not. Our[tokens-per-second guide](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/tokens-per-second) explains what each number means for a user. ## Five mistakes teams make with open-weight models


**Most problems with open-weight models in builders come from treating "open" as one thing.** The model, the license, the host and the builder each change the result. These five mistakes show up again and again:


1. **Sizing hardware by active parameters.** Kimi K3 computes with about 104B parameters per token, but all 2.78T must sit in GPU memory. Plan memory from the checkpoint size in the sizing table above, not from the "A3B" or "active" number.
2. **Reading "open source" as "any use allowed."** MIT and Apache 2.0 have no thresholds, but Kimi K3, the Qwen3.8 flagship, GLM 5.3 and MiniMax M3 add revenue, user or display conditions. Read the license file before you host the weights.
3. **Judging a model by one slow host.** The same Kimi K3 weights ran at 42 and at 422 tokens per second on October 20, 2026. A slow demo can be a host problem, not a model problem.
4. **Pinning a model and forgetting it.** Models leave pickers. In Taskade a retired pin runs on TSK-Auto, so nothing breaks, but your agent is no longer on the model you chose. Check pins when the model list changes.
5. **Trusting a "done" message.** In TSK-1, MiniMax M3 reported an app as ready while 47.2% of its build actions had failed. Open the app, save a record and use it before you ship.


A sixth, smaller one: assuming every model from an open lab is open. Qwen 3.7 Plus and Max are API-only, while Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8 are open-weight. Our[history of Alibaba's Qwen](https://www.taskade.com/blog/alibaba-qwen-history) lays out which is which.

## Frequently Asked Questions


What is an open-weight AI model?


An open-weight model is a model whose trained weights anyone can download, for example Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM 5.2 or gpt-oss. Open weights are not the same as open-source code. The license decides what you can do with the weights, and it differs by model: DeepSeek V4 uses MIT, and Kimi K3 uses Moonshot's own Kimi K3 License. Qwen's smaller open models use Apache 2.0, and the 2.4T Qwen3.8 flagship uses a custom license.


Can I run Kimi K3 without a GPU?


Yes, through a hosted builder or a host API key. Kimi K3 is a 1.56 TB checkpoint that fits one 8x NVIDIA B300 node and does not fit 8x B200 or 8x H100. So most people run it through a host such as Together AI, Fireworks, Baseten or Moonshot, or through a builder that buys tokens from those hosts. In Taskade, Kimi K3 runs on Taskade credits on Max and Enterprise, or on your own Together AI key on Business and up.


Which no-code builder lets me build an app with DeepSeek?


Several. Taskade Genesis offers DeepSeek V4 Pro on Taskade credits on every paid plan, with no API key. MindStudio lists DeepSeek models in its catalog with no API keys required. Dify, n8n and Langflow connect DeepSeek through a DeepSeek node, plugin or component with your own key. Dyad connects it through a provider key or a local Ollama model.


Which AI app builder supports Kimi models?


Taskade runs Kimi K3, Kimi K2.7 Code and Kimi K2.6 on Taskade credits on Max and Enterprise, and a Together AI key on Business and up serves Kimi K3 to custom agents and Ask Agent. Moonshot's own Kimi Build makes full-stack websites on Kimi K3. MindStudio lists Kimi K3 and K2.6. n8n has a Moonshot Kimi Chat Model node, and Dify has an official Moonshot plugin.


Is open source the same as open weights?


No. Open-source code means you can read and change the software. Open weights means you can download the trained model file. A builder can be open source and still call a closed model, and a closed builder can run an open-weight model. This guide is about open-weight models inside hosted builders, not about open-source builder code.


Why are open-weight models often cheaper to run?


Three reasons. Most large open models are mixture-of-experts models, so each token uses only part of the weights: Kimi K3 uses about 104 billion of 2.8 trillion parameters per token. Hybrid attention keeps the memory cache small. And because anyone can host the same weights, many providers compete on price and speed for one model.


Is 40 tokens per second fast enough for an AI app?


For chat, yes. People read at a few words per second, so 40 tokens per second already outruns reading speed. For agents that write long files or run many steps, faster hosts matter more. On October 20, 2026, Artificial Analysis measured Kimi K3 at about 42 tokens per second on Moonshot's own API and about 422 on the fastest host, with the same weights.

How much GPU memory does DeepSeek V4 Pro need?


The official DeepSeek V4 Pro checkpoint on Hugging Face is about 865 GB for 1.6 trillion parameters, with 49 billion active per token. It does not fit an 8x H100 node with 640 GB of GPU memory. It fits an 8x H200 node with about 1,128 GB, or an 8x B200 node with 1.44 TB, with room left for the cache.


Can I build an AI app with Qwen without code?


Yes. The open Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.6 models (27B and 35B-A3B), all Apache 2.0, run locally through Ollama in Dyad or Langflow. Dify connects Qwen through its Tongyi plugin, n8n has a Qwen Cloud chat model node, and MindStudio lists Qwen models with no keys. Is Kimi K3 open source?


Kimi K3 is open-weight. Moonshot published the weights on Hugging Face on July 27, 2026 under the Kimi K3 License, which is not MIT. The license allows use, change and resale, but a Model-as-a-Service business with more than 20 million US dollars of revenue in 12 months needs a separate agreement, and a product with more than 100 million monthly users or 20 million US dollars of monthly revenue must show "Kimi K3" in its interface.


Which open-weight model licenses have no revenue limits?


MIT and Apache 2.0 have no revenue or user thresholds. DeepSeek V4 Pro and V4 Flash, GLM 5.2 and GLM 5.3 Flash use MIT. Qwen3.6, Qwen3.8-27B and gpt-oss use Apache 2.0. Kimi K3, the 2.4T Qwen3.8 flagship, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3 and Nemotron 3 Super use custom licenses with extra conditions, so read each license file before you host the weights yourself.


Can I run an open-source LLM on my laptop?


Only the small ones. gpt-oss-20b has a 14 GB checkpoint that fits a 16 GB GPU, and community 4-bit builds of Qwen3.6-27B or Qwen3.6-35B-A3B fit a 24 GB card. The large open-weight models do not: Kimi K3 is about 1,561 GB and DeepSeek V4 Pro about 865 GB, so they need an 8-GPU server or a hosted builder.


Why is the same open model faster on one host than another?


The weights are the same, but each host picks its own GPUs, parallelism, batch size and speculative decoding. On October 20, 2026, Artificial Analysis measured Kimi K3 at about 422 output tokens per second on the fastest host and about 42 on Moonshot's own API, roughly a 10x spread for one set of weights.
